titulo: Before and after: the capybara, the dinosaur, and the square robot next to the reference drawing — robos-impressos
meta: The capybara, the dinosaur, and the square desktop robot from robos-impressos before (v1.0.2) and after (v1.1.2), next to the reference drawing: images from the same views, similarity measurement by view (IoU), ceiling, target, what changed inside, and the old banner next to the new one.
hero_h1: Did the robot become more like the drawing? See each view, with a number
hero_lead: You choose a robot by how it looks. But between the drawing and the printed part, motors, batteries, and screws come into play, and the robot can turn out very different from what you saw: in the first version, the capybara came out with a long neck. Here you can see the capybara, the dinosaur, and the square desktop robot before and after, next to the reference drawing, and learn to read the ruler that measures how much they came closer.
hero_alt_ref: Reference drawing of the capybara in three-quarter view: orange pear-shaped body, head touching the body, and a green bandana
hero_alt_antes: Render of the capybara in version 1.0.2, in three-quarter view: long neck and upright body
hero_alt_depois: Render of the capybara in version 1.1.2, in three-quarter view: pear-shaped body, head close to the body, and green bandana
hero_cap: The capybara in three-quarter view: the reference drawing, the before render (v1.0.2), and the after render (v1.1.2), both with the same camera. The renders are of the model, not photos: nothing has been printed yet.
resumo: The robos-impressos robots started from a reference drawing. In version 1.0.2, the shells of both animals were made from simple rounded shapes, over a skeleton shared by both, and the result was far from the drawing. In version 1.1.2, the animals’ shapes started coming from a 3D mesh generated on the computer from the drawing itself, and each skeleton was redesigned to fit inside it. The square desktop robot was redesigned without a mesh. To find out whether it really improved, and not just by eye, the project measures the robot’s outline against the drawing’s outline, view by view. The capybara went from [[CAPIVARA_ANTES]] to [[CAPIVARA_DEPOIS]], the dinosaur from [[DINO_ANTES]] to [[DINO_DEPOIS]], and the square robot from [[CUBO_ANTES]] to [[CUBO_DEPOIS]], on a scale from 0 to 1. Both animals passed their target; the square robot improved, but remained below its target. This page shows the images, the numbers, and what the number cannot see.
resumo_nota: The robot images are renders: computer images made from the print files. The reference drawings are the images the project started from, and appear here only for comparison. The other robots and their individual pages are at

ler_h2: IoU: how much one outline overlaps the other
ler_sub: IoU is short for "intersection over union." You place the robot’s silhouette over the drawing’s silhouette and divide the area they share by the area they occupy together.
svg_alt: Two overlapping silhouettes: the part only in the drawing is red, the part only in the robot is blue, and the shared part is green
ler1_p: At 1, the two outlines are identical. At 0, they do not touch at all. On this page, [[CAPIVARA_ANTES]] is the long-necked capybara, and [[CAPIVARA_DEPOIS]] is the capybara whose differences remain along the edge and the bandana bow.
ler2_p: Only the outline, in each drawing view: four for the animals, one for the square robot. Before comparing, both silhouettes are given the same height, their bases are placed on the same line, and their centers are aligned. The robot’s actual size is not part of the calculation.
ler3_p: Color, eyes, mouth, seams, holes, and everything inside the outline. Two robots that look very different from the front can have the same number. That is why the images are here: the number confirms what your eye sees; it does not replace it.
ler4_p: The exact camera used in the drawing is unknown. So the ruler starts from a chosen angle for each view, tests nearby angles (up to 25° on either side, in steps of 5°), and keeps the best one. This accounts for a camera mismatch, but it can also hide small differences. One or two thousandths are noise; you can see a large difference in the images.
ler5_p: It is the raw 3D mesh, generated on the computer from the drawing and measured with the same ruler. Even it does not reach 1: the capybara’s marks [[CAPIVARA_TETO]] and the dinosaur’s, [[DINO_TETO]]. The robot still has wheels, cuts, and clearances: as a rule, it stays below the ceiling. The square robot had no mesh and therefore has no ceiling.
ler6_p: It was set before measuring the after version, so no one could choose the goal by looking at the result: halfway between the before version and the ceiling. The rule applies to the average across views. The target for each view in the tables uses the same calculation for that view. Without a mesh, there is no ceiling: in that case, the target is 0,10 above the before value.
num_teto: ceiling: the raw mesh from the drawing
res_caminho: The robot covered [[PCT]] % of the distance between before and the ceiling.
ref_p: It's the illustration the robot was based on, shown in four views. The ruler compares the robot with each one.

arraste: ↔ on your phone, drag the table sideways

regua_p: This is the image saved by the measurement program. Each row is a view: the reference drawing on the left, the model in the camera view selected by the ruler in the middle, and the two silhouettes overlaid on the right. Red is what only the drawing has, blue is what only the robot has, and green is what they share.

The “adjusted” value is a second measurement, allowing a small margin in scale and position: the tables on this page use IoU without adjustment. The average written in the image title may differ from the table by 1 thousandth due to rounding.

capivara_h2: Capybara: from a long neck to a compact pear shape
capivara_sub: The drawing is a pear: a wide body below, with the head attached to it and no neck. The old skeleton did not allow that.
capivara_m1_t: The shape comes from the drawing
capivara_m1_p: Before, the shell was drawn with simple rounded shapes. Now a 3D mesh generated from the drawing has become the robot's skin: the shell is this skin with 2.4 mm walls, cut into pieces.
capivara_m2_t: A low skeleton, just for her
capivara_m2_p: In the old skeleton, shared by both animals, the neck joint was 185 mm above the ground: that is why the neck was long. In the new one, it was lowered to [[CAPIVARA_PESCOCO]] mm, with the servo that turns the head placed crosswise in the body: its case sits sideways, while the shaft still points upward.
capivara_m3_p: The head is large and sits at the front, and the weight went with it: the center of mass falls in front of the wheel axis. The support ball, which used to be a single one at the back, became two at the front, under the paws.
capivara_m4_p: The torso in two halves, with separate legs and rear, gave way to three large pieces: the whole body, rear door, and collar. Each has a flat base on the build plate and walls that rise close to vertical, so it prints with almost no supports. The collar is the green bandana itself.
capivara_falta: What still separates the capybara from the drawing: the bandana bow at the back of the neck, which was left out because the head, when tilted upward, passes through its place; the flat facet left there; and the edge of the collar-bandana, hands, and apron, which is smooth in the drawing but comes out in steps (jagged) in the model, a known limitation of the mesh cut that the outline does not measure. The shopping list, files, and assembly instructions are at
dino_h2: Dinosaur: legs at the front, tail at the back, and wheels inside the thighs
dino_sub: The dinosaur already started closer to the drawing, and its mesh has a lower ceiling: there was less room left to walk.
dino_m1_t: The shape comes from the drawing
dino_m1_p: As with the capybara, the shell is no longer drawn with simple shapes: it is the skin of the 3D mesh generated from the drawing, with 2.4 mm walls, cut into pieces.
dino_m2_t: A skeleton just for him, with the wheels inside the thighs
dino_m2_p: In the new shape, the legs are at the front and the tail at the back. The wheel axis passes through the thighs, and the shell covers the wheels. With the capybara's skeleton, the dinosaur would tip backward.
dino_m3_t: Support at the back and a shorter neck
dino_m3_p: The center of mass is behind the wheel axis, so the support ball is at the back, under the base of the tail. The neck joint was lowered from 185 to [[DINO_PESCOCO]] mm above the floor, so the neck would be short like in the drawing.
dino_m4_t: Shell printed in vases and an almost straight mouth
dino_m4_p: The body, back, and collar print upright, with the flat edge on the build plate, instead of the torso in two halves. The mesh had an open mouth: the gap was closed, and the mouth opens [[DINO_BOCA]]°. The jaw sits flush against the neck sphere, and each extra degree would make the chin move back against it.
dino_falta: What still separates the dinosaur from the drawing: the closed mouth, the straight band between the legs, and the smooth arms. The shopping list, files, and assembly instructions are at
cubo_h2: Square robot: dark face, rounded corners, and a base that is still too tall
cubo_sub: The square robot reference is a single, small, dimensioned image in three-quarter view. That is why it is measured in one view and has no mesh.
cubo_m1_t: Dark face, as in the reference
cubo_m1_p: The front of the head is a single dark panel, fitted into the head, with the screen and camera behind it. The eyes and mouth shown in the render are the image on the active screen, not a separate part.
cubo_m2_t: The fork moved inside the head
cubo_m2_p: In the previous version, the head was held by a fork on the outside, with the servo horn exposed. Now the fork sits inside the head, at the top of the neck tube, and no mechanism is visible from the outside.
cubo_m3_t: No screws on the front or top
cubo_m3_p: The base cover is secured from below, and the head and battery door from behind. The switch and the charger's USB-C port are also at the back.
cubo_m4_t: Rounded corners and a lower base
cubo_m4_p: The edges of the head are rounded, as in the reference drawing, and the base is lower and wider. Even so, it is still too tall for the drawing: the height of the base is what keeps the number from going higher.
cubo_falta: What still separates the square robot from the drawing: the height of the base and neck. The shopping list, files, and assembly instructions are on the
met_sub: The protocol is the same for the before, after, and mesh. If the ruler changed midway, the numbers would not be comparable.
met_li:
• Each view of the drawing becomes a silhouette: the character cut out from the background.
  • The model is drawn without perspective, using only the printed parts, wheels, and support ball, in a neutral pose and without the phase 2 components.
  • Both silhouettes have the same height (400 pixels), the base is on the same line, and their centers are aligned.
  • The ruler starts from the agreed angle for the view, tests nearby angles (25° on either side, in 5° steps, and five camera heights), and keeps the highest IoU.
  • Each robot's score is the simple average of the measured views.
nota_arred: [[NOME]]: the target is [[ALVO]]. The calculation uses the unrounded values ([[A4]] and [[T4]]). Using the already rounded numbers from the tables ([[A3]] and [[T3]]), it would give [[ALVO_R]]: the difference is only due to rounding.
met_fonte: The numbers come from comparacao/semelhanca.json, saved by the program comum/cad/comparar.py. The full table, with the chosen angle for each view, is at
met_repetir: To repeat the measurement, the reference images are needed. They are not part of the repository: only the ones shown on this page have been published.
q_h2: The square robot on wheels has a score, but not this story
q_p: The square robot on wheels is new and has no drawing of its own. Its score compares it with the drawing of the square desktop robot and is not a target. The explanation is on its page.
